globals.label: ctx
globals.documentation:
The notebook's window onto its configuration and this run.

Variables and secrets are reached through methods rather than injected as
module globals so that a missing key fails with a message naming the key,
and so secret access has one place to pass through.

globals.label: Asset
globals.documentation:
One thing worth scanning.

``id`` is the only field that must be stable across runs: it is what ties
this run's asset to the same asset in the last run, so findings, history and
the scan cache line up. Everything else can change freely.

globals.label: Ref
globals.documentation:
One end of an edge.

``asset`` names something this run produced, by its hash. ``urn`` names an
object by what its *platform* calls it -- which is how a connector points at
a table in a system it does not scan. An unresolved URN is kept and stitched
when the other system is eventually ingested, rather than dropped.

globals.label: FieldMapping
globals.documentation:
One column-level dependency inside a dataset-level flow edge.

``downstream=None`` records an *indirect* dependency -- a column that shaped
which rows came out (an ``ORDER BY``, a ``WHERE``, a join key) without
feeding any particular output column. Keeping it against the dataset instead
of against every output column is what stops indirect dependencies from
fanning out across the whole mapping, and it is the one thing warehouse
lineage tables have no way to say at all.

globals.label: FlowType
globals.detail: TRANSFORM | VIEW | COPY | WRITE | EXPORT | SEND
globals.documentation:
Subtypes of lineage, named so they do not imply a direction.

A verb would: "DERIVED_FROM" reads backwards on an edge that points
downstream. These are the *nature* of the derivation instead, and the
direction is carried by the edge itself.

globals.label: parse
globals.documentation:
Detect a payload's type and extract its text.

Accepts a path, raw bytes, an open binary file, or a ``NotebookFile`` from
``ctx.files``. ``mime_type`` is a hint: it is trusted over sniffing when the
caller already knows, which matters for a payload downloaded from an API
that declared one.

    for file in ctx.files:
        parsed = parse(file)
        yield Asset(id=file.name, content=parsed.text, content_bytes=file.read_bytes())

globals.label: pages
globals.documentation:
Read a payload in pages instead of all at once.

For a Parquet file or a large CSV, ``parse()`` materialises the whole thing
as one string. This yields rows (tabular) or lines (everything else) a page
at a time, so a multi-gigabyte dump can become many assets without ever
being held whole.

    for index, page in enumerate(pages(ctx.file("dump.parquet"))):
        yield Asset(id=f"dump-{index}", content=page, kind="table")

globals.label: flow
globals.detail: (*, upstream: 'Ref', downstream: 'Ref', type: 'FlowType' = <FlowType.TRANSFORM: 'TRANSFORM'>, fields: 'Iterable[FieldMapping] | None' = None, via: 'Ref | None' = None, sql: 'str | None' = None, method: 'Method' = <Method.SYSTEM_CATALOG: 'SYSTEM_CATALOG'>, confidence: 'float | None' = None, evidence: 'dict[str, Any] | None' = None) -> 'Edge'
globals.documentation:
Data moves from ``upstream`` into ``downstream``.

Both ends are keyword-only on purpose: a reversed lineage edge is silently
wrong rather than loudly broken, and it is the mistake everyone makes once.

globals.label: contains
globals.documentation: ``child`` is a part of ``parent`` -- structural, not temporal.

globals.label: references
globals.documentation: ``frm`` points at ``to``. No data moves -- a foreign key is not lineage.

globals.label: same_as
globals.documentation: The same real-world object, seen from two systems.

globals.label: uses
globals.documentation: ``actor`` touched ``target``. Answers "who", not "where did this come from".

globals.label: urn_for
globals.documentation:
The name another system would know this object by.

``urn_for("snowflake", "acme", "PROD", "PUBLIC", "ORDERS")``. The point of
building it here rather than writing the string yourself is that the same
folding rules apply as when the Snowflake connector names that table --
capitalisation and default ports differ between tools, and a URN that
differs by either never matches.

``authority`` is the account, host, workspace or bucket; the rest is the
path within it.

members.label: cursor
members.documentation: What the previous run recorded. Empty on the first run.

members.label: files
members.documentation:
Files uploaded to this source, already downloaded and on local disk.

Empty is a normal state, not an error -- a connector that talks to an API
has no files. Order is by name, so a notebook that pairs files with each
other gets the same pairing every run::

    for file in ctx.files:
        yield Asset(id=file.name, content=file.parse().text)

members.label: folders
members.documentation:
Folders this source was configured with, by name.

The paths are resolved on whatever machine runs the scan: this computer
on desktop, an ephemeral CLI job pod in Kubernetes. In a cluster the
folder has to be mounted into those pods first (the chart's
``api.localFolders``); an unmounted path simply will not exist.

members.label: limit
members.documentation:
How many assets this run wants, or None for "everything".

Read it: a notebook that pushes the limit down to its own API -- a
`LIMIT` clause, a `per_page`, a date filter -- samples at the source
instead of yielding a million records for the runtime to throw away.

members.label: offset
members.documentation:
How many assets this run should skip before the ones it wants.

Non-zero only under AUTOMATIC, where successive runs walk further into
the source. By default the runtime skips them for you -- which means
your ``extract()`` still produces and discards them, and on a large
source that is most of the work.

**Reading this takes over that responsibility.** If you touch
``ctx.offset``, the runtime stops skipping and assumes you applied it
yourself, so push it into your own query::

    def extract():
        for row in api.list(offset=ctx.offset, limit=ctx.limit):
            yield Asset(...)

Read it before you yield anything.

members.label: secret
members.documentation: A configured secret. Values are redacted from output and logs.

members.label: secret_names
members.documentation: Names only. Listing values would defeat redaction.

members.label: set_cursor
members.documentation:
Record where this run got to, for the next run to resume from.

Only meaningful under AUTOMATIC sampling; other strategies ignore it.

members.label: should_abort
members.documentation:
True once the run has been asked to stop.

Check it in long loops. Python cannot be interrupted from outside, so a
loop that ignores this is stopped only by the execution timeout.

Asset.documentation:
One thing worth scanning.

``id`` is the only field that must be stable across runs: it is what ties
this run's asset to the same asset in the last run, so findings, history and
the scan cache line up. Everything else can change freely.

ParsedContent.documentation:
What one file turned out to be.

``error`` is populated rather than raised: a corrupt attachment in the
middle of a long scan should cost that one asset, not the run.

NotebookFile.documentation:
One file this source can read, already on local disk.

The bytes are put there before any notebook code runs -- uploaded files are
downloaded by the parent process, which is what keeps the notebook away from
the API credentials that fetched them. By the time a notebook sees this, it
is an ordinary path.

members.label: open
members.documentation: A binary handle. The caller closes it.

members.label: pages
members.documentation: Read this file a page at a time rather than whole.

members.label: parse
members.documentation: Detect this file's type and extract its text.

members.label: read_bytes
members.documentation: Every byte, in memory. Prefer ``open()`` or ``pages()`` for a big file.
